claims.claim: Philostorgius (born c. 368 at Borissus, Cappadocia); Eunomian (radical Arian) historian; published 425–433.
History ran 12 books (Arius to the 420s); survives only in Photius's epitome.
Philostorgius was an Anomoean Church historian who lived from 368 to approximately 439 AD.

Philostorgius was a member of the Eunomian sect of Christianity, a nonconformist faction deeply opposed to the form of Christianity adopted by the Roman government as the official religion of its empire.
Philostorgius wrote his twelve-book Church History between 425 and 433.
The work covered the period from about 300 to 425, beginning with the heresy of Arius and extending to the death of the usurping emperor John.

Philostorgius wrote his history as a revisionist history of the church and the empire in the fourth and early-fifth centuries, sometimes contradicting and often supplementing what is found in other histories of the period.
The original work is now lost, but the ninth-century historian Photius found a copy in his library in Constantinople and wrote an epitome of it.
Photius's epitome survives in a single manuscript in Oxford.

Photius inveighed throughout his Epitome against Philostorgius as a heretic and impious person, and as a friend and apologist of Arius, Eusebius of Nicomedia, Apollinaris, and other heretics of the fourth and fifth centuries.
